summary: Snorkel AI, spun out of the Stanford AI lab with a decade of data development experience, focuses on solving enterprise data development challenges for fine-tuning foundation models. Off-the-shelf LLMs like Claude, GPT-4, and Gemini rarely meet Fortune 500 enterprises' quality, latency, and cost requirements, so Snorkel develops training data to fine-tune models for the final mile of deployment. RAG is just a starting point; quality, domain-specific data is critical since common instruction tuning datasets lack key domain information. Snorkel's research focuses on three directions: keeping SMEs in the loop while maximizing their time's value, making data development programmatic, scalable, and auditable, and continuous evaluation with domain-specific dynamic benchmarks. Azure's AI infrastructure spans 300+ data centers worldwide with diverse accelerators including AMD, NVIDIA, and first-party silicon (Maia chip), with new AMD MI 300X and upcoming Blackwell on the roadmap. Snorkel's infrastructure stack uses PyTorch, Horovod for multi-node communication, Azure VMs (A100s and H100s), and a shared NFS for data reads and checkpoint writes. Key lessons include balancing node count for ideal batch size, keeping data and nodes co-located, ensuring fast NFS read speeds, monitoring GPU utilization with nvidia-smi, and debugging low utilization by distinguishing multi-node networking issues from single-node data-loading bottlenecks. Snorkel valued Azure's flexibility for long-term on-off compute access, dedicated VMs, dynamically resizable NFS, and ease of use. A cost analysis comparing 2 H100s to 4 A100s (similar cost) showed H100s performing better on both training and inference per dollar, with the simple plug-and-play migration enabling a flywheel of faster iteration through more synthetic data generation. Future Snorkel directions include programmatically utilizing preference signals for data synthesis, scalable data development entry points using rationals and custom taxonomies, and better multimodal retrieval algorithms evaluated on domain-specific datasets.

sections.title: Introduction and Snorkel AI Overview
sections.summary: Hamza introduces himself as an applied research scientist at Snorkel AI working on computer vision and foundation model fine-tuning. Snorkel, originally associated with a hot tub company, focuses on enterprise data development. Off-the-shelf LLMs like Claude, GPT-4, and Gemini don't meet Fortune 500 enterprises' quality, latency, and cost requirements, so Snorkel develops data to fine-tune models for the final mile of deployment.

sections.title: Why Data Development is Hard
sections.summary: RAG is only a starting point; quality domain-specific data is critical. Common instruction tuning datasets are large but lack the specific domain information (e.g., bank policies) needed for enterprise fine-tuning. Snorkel pioneered data development for LLMs, spun out of Stanford AI lab with a decade of experience and many publications.

sections.title: Research Focus and Active Projects
sections.summary: Snorkel's research answers how enterprises can best develop data for custom AI models across three directions: keeping SMEs in the loop, making data development programmatic/scalable/auditable, and continuous domain-specific evaluation. Active projects include fine-grained long context evaluation, enterprise alignment for regulatory compliance, and multimodal alignment using LVLMs to generate synthetic data without manual annotation.

sections.title: Azure AI Infrastructure Overview
sections.summary: Microsoft presenter describes Azure's AI infrastructure: 300+ data centers worldwide, diverse accelerators (AMD, NVIDIA, first-party Maia silicon), optimized topologies for I/O and networking, at supercomputing scale. Learnings from organizations like OpenAI and Mistral are democratized back to customers.

sections.title: Snorkel's Infrastructure Stack on Azure
sections.summary: Snorkel's stack uses PyTorch, Horovod for multi-node communication, Azure VMs (A100s, H100s), and a shared NFS for data reads and checkpoint writes. Workloads range from single-node to dozens of nodes, including DPO alignment, preference optimization, and large-scale distributed multimodal training and inference.

sections.title: Lessons Learned and Best Practices
sections.summary: Key architectural considerations: balance node count for ideal batch size (avoiding too-large batches or underutilization), keep data and nodes co-located to prevent networking bottlenecks during gradient synchronization, ensure fast NFS read speeds to avoid data-loading bottlenecks, and monitor GPU utilization with nvidia-smi to diagnose issues.

sections.title: Debugging GPU Utilization and Cloud Flexibility
sections.summary: When GPU utilization is low, investigate the cause: multi-node setups likely indicate networking issues, while single-node issues usually point to data-loading problems. Don't underestimate reliability, flexibility, and manageability. Snorkel needed long-term flexibility to go on and off compute over extended periods; some cloud providers only offered fixed-duration compute, which didn't suit iterative research workflows.

sections.title: Azure Advantages: Availability, NFS, and Ease of Use
sections.summary: Azure advantages include dedicated VMs with on-demand capacity adjustment, consistent reliability, good NFS throughput with dynamically resizable storage, and ease of use with clear documentation. The setup worked reliably once configured, minimizing ongoing maintenance burden. NFS can be scaled up for more data or down to avoid overpaying.

sections.title: H100 vs A100 Cost Analysis
sections.summary: A cost analysis comparing 2 H100s to 4 A100s (similar cost) showed H100s performing better on both training and inference per dollar. The migration was a simple plug-and-play change. Faster inference enables more synthetic data generation, higher model accuracy, and a flywheel of faster iteration critical for development. A Q&A clarified that training and inference batch sizes were kept fixed across hardware comparisons.

sections.title: What's Next: Azure Silicon Roadmap and Snorkel Research Directions
sections.summary: Azure is adopting new silicon including Maia AI accelerator, AMD MI 300X with high-bandwidth memory, and upcoming Blackwell, with Nvidia now releasing almost twice yearly versus previously every two years. Snorkel's future directions include programmatically utilizing preference signals for data synthesis and curation, developing scalable data development entry points using rationals and custom taxonomies, and building better multimodal retrieval algorithms evaluated on domain-specific datasets, all on Azure AI infrastructure.
